hints: Focus on what the word specificity means, it is about being selective rather than just being a catalyst.
Think lock and key, maltase has an active site shaped to fit maltose, so will it fit many other substrates?
Look for the option that says maltase acts on only its own reaction and not on lots of different reactions.
walkthrough:
**Recall what specificity means**

Think of an enzyme like a special key that only fits one lock. Specificity means it will only bind its own substrate and catalyse its own reaction.

Chemical reaction shown:
$$\text{maltose} + \text{water} \xrightarrow{\text{maltase}} \text{glucose}$$

**Separate general properties from specificity**

Many statements are true about all enzymes, but they do not explain being selective. Being a protein, working best at a certain pH, and lowering $E_a$ are true for enzymes in general.

**Identify the selective statement**

Only one statement says maltase is choosy and speeds up just a small number of reactions. That is the definition of specificity, so that is the answer.

options.A: This is true about enzymes in general, maltase is a protein catalyst, but it does not describe specificity. It does not tell us that maltase is selective for maltose.
options.B: This describes optimum pH, which is about conditions for maximum activity. It is true that enzymes are pH sensitive, but it does not explain why maltase only acts on maltose.
options.C: This describes how all catalysts work, by providing an alternative route of lower activation energy. It applies to every enzyme reaction, not to the selective nature of maltase.
options.D: This is exactly what specificity means. Because its active site is complementary to maltose, maltase only catalyses this hydrolysis and a very small number of similar reactions, not all reactions.
